response.query: How should we design temporal sampling and resampling strategies to robustly handle variable frame rates and asynchronous metadata while minimizing aliasing?
response.answer: Design temporal sampling with a rate at least twice the highest frequency component to avoid aliasing; use interpolation for asynchronous metadata; employ temporal anti-aliasing techniques to minimize artifacts.

results.content:
Title: Aliasing issues | TV Tech
With the growing use of multiple video formats, a fundamental understanding of sampling rate conversion will provide insight into the quality and operation of format converters. It is well known that a signal must be sampled at a rate at least twice as high as the highest frequency component — Nyquist's theorem — or aliasing will result. When sampled at less than that, the resulting signal will have a frequency less than that of the original, meaning it has been aliased, and no amount of processing will retrieve the original signal. Another way of looking at this is that the sampling process creates repeat spectra in the frequency domain, i.e., the original signal spectrum will repeat, centered at multiples of the sampling rate. If one were to simply throw away every other sample (a process called decimation) when the original image had frequency components out to one-half the original sampling rate, then this decimation would result in aliasing in the final image. It's important to realize that lowering the sample rate is, in effect, resampling the image. When converting from a lower to a higher resolution image (or when increasing the audio sampling rate), an upsampling process is used. In the frequency domain, this creates repeat spectra between the original signal and the new sampling rate. The previous examples illustrate the process of changing the sampling rate by an integer factor. But with sampling rates much lower than those needed for video, the overall complexity (and cost) will be much less. With audio signals, there may also be a more frequent need for asynchronous rate conversion (e.g., where the source and destination sampling rates are unrelated). One such case could be where the destination requires a specific sample rate, locked to a reference frequency, and the source sampling rate is determined by a free-running clock, as in a recorder. Assuming one wants to keep the signal in its digital form, the conversion system may have to convert on the fly, with interpolation or decimation carried out as needed on a sample-by-sample basis. In future articles, we'll discuss how sampling rate conversion is used in format conversion, and how video artifacts arise from the different elements.

results.title: Temporal anti-aliasing - Wikipedia
results.content: **Temporal anti-aliasing** (**TAA**) refers to two distinct forms of anti-aliasing in computer graphics. The commonly understood meaning is a specific technique that removes spatial aliasing from an image, using data from multiple frames, and is used in video games and real-time rendering. The modern definition of TAA is a spatial anti-aliasing technique for real-time computer graphics that reuses information from previously rendered frames to remove aliasing, such as jaggies, from the current frame. TAA popularized in video games in the 2010s, with two early examples being Halo: Reach and Crysis 2, and is now the most common form of spatial anti-aliasing in real-time rendering and game engines. Multisample anti-aliasing (MSAA), which was previously the most common real-time spatial anti-aliasing method, does not work well with deferred shading, which is needed for a number of common rendering techniques. This results in temporal aliasing: moving objects can appear to jump or flash between frames as their position changes. 5. ^ ***a*** ***b*** ***c*** ***d*** ***e*** Ziyad Barakat "Temporal Anti Aliasing – Step by Step".
